title: Camillus de Lellis (mid-July)
hook: a gambler and soldier who founded nursing brothers with red crosses on their habits

segments.voice: Yesterday, Our Lady of Mount Carmel and the brown scapular. Your line was under her mantle.

A young man with a bad leg and a worse habit. He's been a soldier for hire, fighting wherever there's pay. Between wars he plays cards and dice, and he loses. Tradition says he once gambled away nearly everything he owned, down to the shirt on his back. To eat, he works as a laborer, then as an attendant in a Roman hospital, the kind of place for people nobody expects to get well. He's dismissed for gambling. So how does that man end up founding an order of nurses?
screen: `A SOLDIER FOR HIRE.` → `CARDS, DICE, AND DEBT.` → `DISMISSED FROM A HOSPITAL.`

segments.voice: Camillus de Lellis didn't turn around all at once. Tradition says the change began while he worked as a laborer for Capuchin friars, when one of them took him aside and spoke to him plainly about his life. He was taken in as a novice, but the wound on his leg, which never healed, opened again, and the friars sent him away. So he went back to the hospital, and this time he stayed. He watched how the sick were treated: hired attendants who didn't care, patients left dirty, hungry, alone. He began to gather a few men who would nurse the sick the way a mother nurses her only child, a picture tradition gives in his own words. That little group became an order, called the Ministers of the Infirm, and Camillus became a priest. Then came the red cross. His brothers wore a large red cross on the chest of their black habits, so anyone, in a ward or a street, could see who had come to serve. They went into hospitals, into the homes of the dying, onto battlefields. Under all of it was the Gospel scene of the last judgment, where Jesus counts care for the sick as care done to himself. For Camillus, that was not a figure of speech: the patient in the bed was Christ. And the old gambler kept something from his past. He never stopped taking risks. He just changed what he bet on.
screen: `A FRIAR SPEAKS PLAINLY.` · `BACK TO THE HOSPITAL, TO STAY.` · `A RED CROSS ON A BLACK HABIT.` · `THE PATIENT IS CHRIST.` · then, large: `HE CHANGED WHAT HE BET ON.`

segments.voice: Go back to a time you were sick or hurt, a hospital bed, a fever at home, a long recovery, and find the one who took care of you: a nurse whose name you never learned, a parent, a friend who brought soup. Stay with their hands and their voice, and what they did that you couldn't. If you pray, thank God for them and ask a blessing on their work; if you don't, hold them in gratitude.
Camillus, once a soldier and gambler. He became a priest and gathered brothers to nurse the sick, marked with a red cross on their habits.
Your line: the red cross. Care for the sick can take real courage. That's day one thousand nine.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Camillus de Lellis in mid-July as a patron of the sick, nurses and hospitals, and his order, the Camillians, still serves the sick wearing the red cross.

A doctor in Rome who built the first hospital ever and trained all its nurses himself.

chat.meaning: Camillus, once a soldier and gambler, stayed at the hospital, gathered men to nurse the sick, and marked them with a red cross. To him the patient was Christ.

notes: Gambling away nearly everything 'down to the shirt on his back' is given as tradition; confirm.
Turning point while working for Capuchins, refusal because of his leg wound, return to the hospital in Rome (San Giacomo degli Incurabili, not named): confirm.
'Nurse the sick the way a mother nurses her only child' is paraphrased as a picture his followers remember him using; confirm attribution.
Order's name given as 'Ministers of the Infirm'; red cross on black habit. No link to the later Red Cross organization is claimed; keep it that way.
Feast left as 'mid-July' per index (14 July in the general calendar; 18 July in some national calendars). Confirm.
Matthew 25 is paraphrased, not quoted, because day 1001 (Aloysius Gonzaga) already quotes 25:36.
Editor pass: reworded 'took that literally' (day 1001 used the same line about Matthew 25) in teach and trapdoor; the mother-and-only-child picture now attributed to tradition.
